metadata.title: Leg Entanglement Top Position | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Leg Entanglement Top Position in BJJ. Complete guide covering control, leg locks, and transitions. Dominant leg entanglement with 70% retention rate.

overview: Leg Entanglement Top Position represents a category of advanced positional control in modern BJJ where the top practitioner controls and attacks their opponent's lower body through various configurations of leg positioning and entanglement. These positions form the foundation of modern leg lock systems, characterized by superior control mechanics that isolate specific joints (ankle, knee, hip) while maintaining positional dominance. The top player has secured an entanglement configuration that provides both control and attacking opportunities, typically involving their legs wrapping, hooking, or triangling around the opponent's leg or legs. This position family has revolutionized modern no-gi grappling, with systematic approaches developed by John Danaher, Craig Jones, and others transforming leg attacks from opportunistic submissions into a comprehensive positional hierarchy. Success in top leg entanglements requires understanding the biomechanical principles of joint isolation, recognizing the specific finishing mechanics for different leg locks, and maintaining proper positioning to prevent escapes or counters. The position offers multiple pathways to finishing submissions (heel hooks, kneebar variations, ankle locks) while also providing transition opportunities to other dominant positions if the opponent defends successfully.
state_invariants: Top practitioner maintains superior positioning with at least one of opponent's legs controlled through leg entanglement (wrapping, hooking, or triangling configuration)
Top player's upper body positioning allows weight distribution and base maintenance while hands control opponent's leg or establish grips on foot/ankle for submission attacks
Opponent's mobility is restricted through the specific entanglement configuration, with their leg(s) isolated and controlled, typically with their knee line compromised or ankle exposed
Top practitioner's hips are positioned to generate rotational force or extension pressure against isolated joint (ankle, knee, or hip depending on specific configuration)
Clear line of attack exists to at least one submission target (heel, ankle, knee) based on the specific entanglement variant being employed
prerequisites: Successful entry from standing position, open guard passing, or transition from other top positions
Control established over at least one of opponent's legs through specific entanglement configuration
Opponent's defensive structure compromised allowing leg isolation
Top practitioner's base and balance sufficient to maintain position during opponent's escape attempts
Understanding of specific entanglement variant mechanics and associated submission opportunities
key_principles: Maintain constant pressure and control on the isolated leg to prevent opponent from clearing the entanglement and recovering guard
Keep hips close to the attack point (foot, ankle, or knee) to maximize control and finishing leverage while minimizing escape opportunities
Control opponent's upper body or free leg to prevent them from turning into you or establishing defensive frames
Understand the specific biomechanics of your entanglement variant to recognize which submissions are available and which transitions are necessary
Maintain proper angle relative to opponent's knee line to prevent them from straightening their leg and escaping the entanglement
Use grip fighting on the foot/ankle to control opponent's ability to spin or rotate out of danger
Recognize when to transition between entanglement variants based on opponent's defensive reactions and positioning changes

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to turn away and clear the knee line
Opponent tries to pull their leg straight and extract
Opponent rolls toward their trapped leg
Opponent extends their leg attempting to push you away
Opponent turns into you giving up their back to escape leg attack
Opponent's foot becomes exposed during escape attempt

decision_tree.condition: If opponent has their knee bent and is defending by keeping their heel hidden from attack
If opponent extends their leg trying to create distance and push away
If opponent's heel becomes exposed with proper inside or outside positioning
If opponent turns away from you exposing their back to escape the leg entanglement
If opponent successfully clears the knee line and begins to escape

common_errors.error: Allowing too much space between hips and the target joint (ankle or knee)
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can create distance, rotate their leg out of danger, and eventually escape the entanglement completely
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant hip pressure toward the attack point, keeping your hips glued to their leg and closing any gaps that develop during transitions

common_errors.error: Neglecting to control opponent's upper body or free leg during submission attempts
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can establish defensive frames, turn into you, or use their free leg to push and create escape opportunities
common_errors.correction: Use grips on the belt, collar, or pants to control upper body positioning, and actively manage their free leg with your hands or legs

common_errors.error: Forcing submissions without proper angle and positioning relative to the knee line
common_errors.consequence: Ineffective submission attempts that allow opponent to defend easily and potentially counter or escape the position
common_errors.correction: Ensure your body is positioned at the correct angle for the specific submission before applying pressure, following the systematic entries taught in leg lock systems

common_errors.error: Remaining static in one entanglement configuration when opponent is successfully defending
common_errors.consequence: Opponent eventually finds the escape pathway for that specific configuration and recovers guard or worse
common_errors.correction: Flow between different entanglement variants based on opponent's reactions, transitioning from ashi to saddle to 50-50 as defenses require

common_errors.error: Gripping the foot with incorrect hand positioning that telegraphs the submission
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recognizes the attack early and can defend by hiding their heel, straightening their leg, or spinning
common_errors.correction: Use deceptive grips and maintain control positions that allow multiple submission pathways, only committing to specific grips at the moment of finishing

common_errors.error: Ignoring positional hierarchy and going directly for low-percentage submissions
common_errors.consequence: Failed submission attempts that result in loss of position and opportunity to finish
common_errors.correction: Follow the systematic approach of establishing dominant entanglement first, then transitioning to better variants before committing to submission attempts

common_errors.error: Not understanding the specific biomechanics and danger zones of each leg lock variation
common_errors.consequence: Applying dangerous submissions incorrectly, potentially causing injury to training partners or failing in competition due to poor technique
common_errors.correction: Study the biomechanical principles of each submission thoroughly, practice with control and awareness, and only train heel hooks with experienced practitioners

training_drills.name: Entanglement Configuration Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Partner starts with leg entangled in basic ashi position. Top player flows through all major entanglement variants (inside ashi, outside ashi, saddle, 50-50) based on bottom player's defensive movements. Focus on smooth transitions and maintaining constant control throughout configuration changes. 5 minutes per partner.

training_drills.name: Submission Chain Development
training_drills.description: From established leg entanglement, practice transitioning between different submission attacks based on partner's defensive reactions. When heel is hidden, transition to kneebar. When leg extends, switch between ankle lock and toe hold. When partner turns away, recognize back exposure. Build automatic response patterns. 3-minute rounds.

training_drills.name: Positional Sparring from Entanglement
training_drills.description: Start in basic ashi garami top position with 30 seconds on shot clock. Top player works for submission or better entanglement position. Bottom player works for escape to guard recovery. Reset and switch every 2 minutes. Emphasizes real-time decision making and pressure maintenance under resistance.

training_drills.name: Entry Sequence Repetition
training_drills.description: Partner presents various top positions (headquarters, knee cut, leg drag). Top player practices recognizing entry opportunities and executing smooth transitions to leg entanglement positions. Focus on timing, angle creation, and securing control immediately upon entry. 10 repetitions per entry type.

training_drills.name: Escape Prevention Drill
training_drills.description: Partner attempts specific escapes from leg entanglement (hip escape, knee clearing, rolling escape, technical standup). Top player practices recognizing and countering each escape attempt with appropriate position adjustments or submission attacks. Builds defensive awareness and counter-transition timing. 5 minutes continuous.

expert_insights.danaher: The leg entanglement positions represent a complete positional hierarchy that mirrors the traditional upper body hierarchy of guard, half guard, side control, mount, and back control. Each entanglement configuration has specific control characteristics and submission opportunities, and understanding the systematic transitions between them is essential for effective leg lock attacking. The key principle is that position comes before submission - you must first establish dominant control through proper entanglement before attempting to finish. The biomechanical principle underlying all successful leg entanglements is the isolation of the target joint through creating opposing forces: your legs control their leg while your upper body prevents compensatory movement. Master the entries from top positions first, as controlling from top allows you to maintain positional dominance even if submissions are defended. The heel hook is the king of leg locks due to its devastating effectiveness, but it requires perfect positional control and understanding of the knee line concept - your ability to break their knee line determines which submissions become available.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In modern competition, leg entanglements from top position are absolutely essential for high-level success, especially in no-gi where the lack of gi grips makes traditional passing more difficult. I use leg entanglements as both a passing tool and a finishing system - when opponents defend my passes by creating distance with their legs, I enter into leg entanglement positions that give me both control and submission threats. The most important skill is recognizing which entanglement variant you're in and knowing the highest percentage submission for that specific configuration. Don't waste time forcing low-percentage attacks from poor positions. If you're in outside ashi and they're defending the outside heel hook well, transition to inside ashi or saddle rather than continuing to fight a losing battle. The competitive advantage of leg entanglements is that many opponents still don't understand the positions well, so they make defensive errors that create easy finishes. My approach is to establish the entanglement, secure the dominant variant (usually saddle), then attack with maximum efficiency. Time management is crucial in competition - know when to finish from legs and when to abandon for positional advancement.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Leg entanglements completely changed the game when we started really developing them in the 10th Planet system, especially from positions like the lockdown where you already have leg control. The beauty of top leg entanglements is that you can attack them from anywhere - failed guard passes, scrambles, even from bottom positions if you're creative. What I love about the leg game is that it forces opponents to deal with threats they're not comfortable with, creating openings everywhere. My philosophy is to stay unpredictable - don't just hunt heel hooks, use the leg entanglement to threaten multiple attacks and transitions. From top leg positions, I'm always looking at the back take opportunities when they turn away to defend the legs. The leg game pairs perfectly with the truck position and twister mechanics we developed - both systems use leg control to create devastating attacks. The key innovation in modern leg locks is understanding that you don't need to finish the first submission you enter - use the threat to create reactions, then capitalize on their defensive movements with chain attacks. Train the positions with the same intensity you train traditional top positions, because in no-gi they're equally important for controlling and finishing opponents.
